verses.text: Beloved, this is now my second letter to you. Both of them are reminders to stir you to wholesome thinking
by recalling what was foretold by the holy prophets and commanded by our Lord and Savior through your apostles.
Most importantly, you must understand that in the last days scoffers will come, scoffing and following their own evil desires.
"Where is the promise of His coming?" they will ask. "Ever since our fathers fell asleep, everything continues as it has from the beginning of creation."
But they deliberately overlook the fact that long ago by God's word the heavens existed and the earth was formed out of water and by water,
through which the world of that time perished in the flood.
And by that same word, the present heavens and earth are reserved for fire, being kept for the day of judgment and destruction of ungodly men.
Beloved, do not let this one thing escape your notice: With the Lord a day is like a thousand years, and a thousand years are like a day.
The Lord is not slow in keeping His promise as some understand slowness, but is patient with you, not wanting anyone to perish but everyone to come to repentance.
But the Day of the Lord will come like a thief. The heavens will disappear with a roar, the elements will be destroyed by fire, and the earth and its works will be laid bare.
Since everything will be destroyed in this way, what kind of people ought you to be? You ought to conduct yourselves in holiness and godliness
as you anticipate and hasten the coming of the day of God, when the heavens will be destroyed by fire and the elements will melt in the heat.
But in keeping with God's promise, we are looking forward to a new heaven and a new earth, where righteousness dwells.
Therefore, beloved, as you anticipate these things, make every effort to be found at peace—spotless and blameless in His sight.
Consider also that our Lord's patience brings salvation, just as our beloved brother Paul also wrote you with the wisdom God gave him.

He writes this way in all his letters, speaking in them about such matters. Some parts of his letters are hard to understand, which ignorant and unstable people distort, as they do the rest of the Scriptures, to their own destruction.
Therefore, beloved, since you already know these things, be on your guard so that you will not be carried away by the error of the lawless and fall from your secure standing.
But grow in the grace and knowledge of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ. To Him be the glory both now and to the day of eternity. Amen.

context.author: Simon Peter, writing what he calls his second letter to them (3:1); the authorship is debated.
context.audience: Readers to whom he has already written once (3:1), probably the churches of 1 Peter.
context.setting: Peter writes this second letter to stir up their sincere minds. Scoffers will ask, “Where is the promise of his coming?” Peter reminds them that God made the world by his word and judged it by water, and will judge it by fire. A day is as a thousand years to the Lord. His patience is salvation, and he calls them to holy lives.
context.custom: The Day of the Lord was an old warning in Israel (Amos 5:18-20; Zephaniah 1:14-18). The thief is a picture from Jesus (Matthew 24:43) that Paul also used (1 Thessalonians 5:2). Some scholars compare the melting elements with Stoic ideas of a world that ends in fire, but Peter ends not in a cycle but in new heavens and a new earth where righteousness dwells (3:13).
context.timelineImmediate: The letter ends here. Tradition says Peter died at Rome under Nero, but the New Testament does not describe his death.
context.timelineBible: A day with the Lord as a thousand years (3:8) echoes Psalm 90:4. The new heavens and new earth (3:13) recall Isaiah 65:17 and 66:22. Verses 15-16 name Paul and his letters, and verse 16 places them with the rest of the Scriptures.
context.sparkNotes: In the last days scoffers will come, saying, “Where is the promise of his coming?” But the Lord is not slow to fulfill his promise as some count slowness, but is patient toward you, not wishing that any should perish, but that all should reach repentance. The day of the Lord will come like a thief, and the heavens will pass away with a roar. Since all these things are to be dissolved, what sort of people ought you to be? According to his promise we are waiting for new heavens and a new earth in which righteousness dwells. Grow in the grace and knowledge of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ.

overview.summary: Scoffers deny Christ’s return, but the Lord is patient so more will repent. The day will come, and believers wait for new heavens and a new earth.
overview.settingLine: Peter writes near the end of his life.

history.t: Peter calls Paul our beloved brother and says his letters have some things that are hard to understand, which the ignorant and unstable distort, as they do the rest of the Scriptures (3:15-16). Papyrus 46, from about AD 200, is a book of Paul’s letters, so they were being copied and read together early.

The scoffers say nothing has changed since creation (3:4). Peter answers that the world once perished by water and is now kept for fire (3:5-7). Genesis 6-9 tells of the flood, and Old Testament pictures of judgment by fire include Zephaniah 1:18 and Malachi 4:1.

Peter says the Lord is not slow about his promise but patient, not wanting anyone to perish but all to come to repentance (3:9). Paul makes a similar point about God’s kindness and patience in Romans 2:4.

customs.t: A thief comes without warning, and that is Peter’s picture of the Day of the Lord (3:10). Jesus used the same picture (Matthew 24:43-44), and so did Paul (1 Thessalonians 5:2).

The Greek word for elements (stoicheia) can mean the basic parts of the physical world, such as earth, air, fire and water, or the heavenly bodies. Commentators differ over which Peter means in 3:10 and 3:12.

archaeology.t: Papyrus 46 is a papyrus book of Paul’s letters, usually dated to about AD 200. It shows that his letters were being copied and read together early, which fits Peter’s mention of all his letters (3:15-16). Whether Peter knew them as a collection is debated.

Another leaf of Papyrus 72, the 3rd or 4th century book that holds 1 and 2 Peter and Jude, has the closing part of this letter. The doubts that Origen, Eusebius and Jerome report did not stop 2 Peter from being copied in Egypt.

Peter’s new heavens and new earth (3:13) recall Isaiah 65:17 and 66:22. The Great Isaiah Scroll from Qumran, about 125-100 BC, holds the whole book of Isaiah, so the prophecy Peter knew was already in scrolls like it.

overview.discussion: Peter says God’s patience is salvation. Who in my life am I tempted to give up on, and how does God’s patience change that?
overview.book: The second letter of Peter · 3 chapters. Peter’s last words, written as he expects to die soon.

historicalImage.caption: A folio of Papyrus 46, a papyrus book of Paul’s letters usually dated to about AD 200, though some scholars place it earlier. Peter calls Paul our beloved brother and says his letters, like the rest of the Scriptures, are twisted by the ignorant and unstable (3:15-16).

currentImage.caption: Mount Ararat, with Great and Little Ararat, seen across the Ararat plain in Armenia. Genesis 8:4 says the ark came to rest on the mountains of Ararat. Peter recalls that God preserved Noah, a preacher of righteousness, when the flood came on the ungodly world (2:5; 3:6). The Bible names a range of mountains and not this peak.
